questions.stem: You want to invite a friend to watch a film together on Saturday.
questions.explanation: 「土曜日にいっしょにえいがを見ませんか。」 A day of the week takes 「に」, and the film is the object, so 「を」. 「〜ませんか」 is a polite invitation; 「見ましたか」 would ask whether they had already seen it.

build.translation: Would you like to watch a film together on Saturday?

questions.stem: You want to invite a friend to play tennis on Sunday.
questions.explanation: 「日曜日にテニスをしませんか。」 Sports are played with 「する」, so 「テニスをします」, and the invitation ending 「ませんか」 goes on the ます-stem 「し」.

build.translation: Would you like to play tennis on Sunday?

questions.stem: You want to ask a friend whether they would like to go shopping tomorrow.
questions.explanation: 「あした、買い物に行きませんか。」 「あした」 is a relative time word, so it takes no particle. 「買い物に行く」 is 'go shopping', with 「に」 marking the purpose of going.

build.translation: Would you like to go shopping tomorrow?

questions.stem: You want to invite a classmate to eat lunch together at lunchtime.
questions.explanation: 「昼休みに、いっしょにおべんとうを食べませんか。」 「いっしょに」 is a fixed adverb, 'together', and never takes 「で」. The ending goes on the ます-stem: 「食べ」 + 「ませんか」.

build.translation: Shall we eat our lunch together at lunchtime?

questions.stem: You want to invite a friend to go and see the fireworks on Friday night.
questions.explanation: 「金曜日の夜、はなびを見に行きませんか。」 The ます-stem plus 「に行く」 means 'go to do': 「見に行く」, 'go to see'. 「金曜日の夜」 joins the two nouns with 「の」.

build.translation: Would you like to go and see the fireworks on Friday night?

questions.stem: You are arranging to meet a friend in front of the station at three o'clock.
questions.explanation: 「三時に駅の前で会いましょう。」 A clock time takes 「に」, and meeting is an action, so the place takes 「で」. 「駅の前に」 would describe where something is, not where something happens.

build.translation: Let's meet in front of the station at three o'clock.

questions.stem: Once the meeting time is fixed, you suggest that everyone then goes by school bus.
questions.explanation: 「それから、学校のバスで行きましょう。」 「それから」 adds the next step of the plan, and a means of transport takes 「で」: 「バスで行く」, 'go by bus'.

build.translation: After that, let's go by school bus.

questions.stem: A friend suggests going to the beach. You reply that it sounds good and suggest going.
questions.explanation: 「いいですね。行きましょう。」 「いいですね」 welcomes the idea, and 「ましょう」 on the ます-stem 「行き」 makes 'let's go'.

build.translation: Sounds good. Let's go!

questions.stem: You are confirming the arrangement back to a friend: Friday at half past three, in front of the station.
questions.explanation: 「じゃあ、金曜日の三時半に、駅の前ですね。」 「じゃあ」 opens a summary, and 「ですね」 checks that you both agree. 「金曜日の三時半」 joins day and time with 「の」, and only the time takes 「に」.

build.translation: So, that's Friday at half past three, in front of the station.

questions.stem: You want to tell a friend that you have eaten sushi in Japan.
questions.explanation: 「日本ですしを食べたことがあります。」 Experience is the plain past 「食べた」 plus 「ことがあります」. 「こと」 is a thing, not a living being, so it takes 「あります」, never 「います」.

build.translation: I have eaten sushi in Japan.

questions.stem: You want to tell a friend that you have ridden a train in Tokyo.
questions.explanation: 「とうきょうで電車にのったことがあります。」 「のる」 (ride) marks the vehicle with 「に」, because you get on to it. Its plain past is 「のった」.

build.translation: I have ridden a train in Tokyo.

questions.stem: You want to tell a friend that you have climbed Mount Fuji with your family.
questions.explanation: 「家族とふじさんにのぼったことがあります。」 「と」 is 'with' a person, and 「にのぼる」 is 'climb up to'. 「のぼる」 is an う-verb, so its past is 「のぼった」.

build.translation: I have climbed Mount Fuji with my family.

questions.stem: You want to tell a friend that you have written an email in Japanese.
questions.explanation: 「日本語でメールを書いたことがあります。」 The language you use is a means, so it takes 「で」. 「書く」 ends in 「く」, so its past is 「書いた」.

build.translation: I have written an email in Japanese.

questions.stem: You want to tell a friend that you have never been to Japan yet.
questions.explanation: 「まだ日本に行ったことがありません。」 「まだ」 with a negative is 'not yet'. 「行く」 keeps its exception in the past, 「行った」, and the negative of 「あります」 is 「ありません」.

build.translation: I have never been to Japan yet.

questions.stem: You want to ask a Japanese exchange student whether they have ever eaten a meat pie.
questions.explanation: 「ミートパイを食べたことがありますか。」 Adding 「か」 turns the experience pattern into a question: 'have you ever …?'.

build.translation: Have you ever eaten a meat pie?

questions.stem: You explain that because it is raining, you will read a book at home.
questions.explanation: 「雨がふっているから、うちで本を読みます。」 「から」 after the reason means 'because'. Reading is an action, so the place takes 「で」.

build.translation: It's raining, so I'll read a book at home.

questions.stem: You explain that you will study today because you have a test tomorrow.
questions.explanation: 「あしたテストがあるから、今日はべんきょうします。」 A test is an event, so it takes 「ある」, not 「いる」. The plain form 「ある」 goes before 「から」.

build.translation: I have a test tomorrow, so I'll study today.

questions.stem: You tell a friend that you are tired, so you will go to bed early.
questions.explanation: 「つかれたから、早く寝ます。」 「早い」 becomes the adverb 「早く」 before a verb. 「つかれた」 is past in form but describes how you feel now.

build.translation: I'm tired, so I'll go to bed early.

questions.stem: You say that you often come to this shop because it is cheap.
questions.explanation: 「この店は安いから、よく来ます。」 An い-adjective goes straight before 「から」; 「だ」 is only for nouns and な-adjectives. 「よく」 here means 'often'.

build.translation: This shop is cheap, so I often come here.

questions.stem: You explain that fish is good for the body, so you eat it every day.
questions.explanation: 「魚は体にいいから、毎日食べます。」 「体にいい」 is the set phrase 'good for you'. 「毎日」 is a time word that takes no particle.

build.translation: Fish is good for you, so I eat it every day.

questions.stem: You explain that you study Japanese because you like Japanese anime.
questions.explanation: 「日本のアニメが好きだから、日本語をべんきょうしています。」 「好き」 is a な-adjective, so it needs 「だ」 before 「から」: 「好きだから」. 「好きから」 is the most common slip.

options: べんきょうしています。
べんきょうしましょう。
べんきょうしてください。

build.translation: I like Japanese anime, so I'm studying Japanese.

questions.stem: You say that you shop at the convenience store because it is convenient.
questions.explanation: 「べんりだから、コンビニで買い物をします。」 「べんり」 is a な-adjective, so it takes 「だから」. Shopping is an action, so the shop takes 「で」.

build.translation: It's convenient, so I shop at the convenience store.

questions.stem: A friend asks why you can't come. You explain that it is because you have your part-time job.
questions.explanation: 「アルバイトがあるからです。」 The answer to 「どうして」 ends in 「からです」. A shift is something you have, so 「アルバイトがある」.

build.translation: It's because I have my part-time job.

questions.stem: You ask the teacher if you may go to the toilet.
questions.explanation: 「トイレに行ってもいいですか。」 The て-form plus 「もいいですか」 asks permission. 「行く」 has the irregular て-form 「行って」.

build.translation: May I go to the toilet?

questions.stem: At a temple, you ask whether you may take a photo here.
questions.explanation: 「ここでしゃしんをとってもいいですか。」 「とる」 is an う-verb ending in 「る」, so its て-form is 「とって」. Taking a photo is an action, so 「ここで」.

build.translation: May I take a photo here?

questions.stem: You explain a class rule to a visitor: students must not use smartphones during lessons.
questions.explanation: 「じゅぎょう中に、スマホをつかってはいけません。」 「〜てはいけません」 forbids. 「つかう」 ends in 「う」, so its て-form is 「つかって」.

build.translation: We must not use smartphones during lessons.

questions.stem: You tell an exchange student that students here have to do homework every day.
questions.explanation: 「毎日、しゅくだいをしなければなりません。」 The ない-form of 「する」 is 「しない」, and 「しない」 becomes 「しなければ」. 「なりません」 completes 'must'.

build.translation: We have to do homework every day.

questions.stem: You tell a friend that you don't have to go to school on Saturday.
questions.explanation: 「土曜日は学校に行かなくてもいいです。」 「行かない」 becomes 「行かなくて」, and 「もいいです」 makes 'it's fine not to'. 「いけません」 would turn it into a ban.

build.translation: I don't have to go to school on Saturday.

questions.stem: You remind your classmates not to talk loudly on the bus.
questions.explanation: 「バスの中で大きなこえで話さないでください。」 A negative request is the ない-form plus 「でください」. 「話す」 is an う-verb, so 「話さない」.

build.translation: Please don't talk loudly on the bus.

questions.stem: You explain the library rule to a new student: eating is not allowed in the library.
questions.explanation: 「としょかんで食べてはいけません。」 Eating is an action, so the place takes 「で」. 「食べる」 is a る-verb, so the て-form is simply 「食べて」.

build.translation: You must not eat in the library.

questions.stem: You tell a friend that you plan to go to Japan in the summer holidays.
questions.explanation: 「夏休みに日本に行くつもりです。」 「つもり」 follows the dictionary form: 「行くつもり」. It states a plan you have already decided on.

build.translation: I plan to go to Japan in the summer holidays.

questions.stem: You explain that in the future you plan to become a doctor.
questions.explanation: 「しょうらい、いしゃになるつもりです。」 'Become' is 「〜になる」, with 「に」 on what you become. 「しょうらい」 points to the future, so 「きのう」 and 「先週」 do not fit.

build.translation: In the future, I plan to become a doctor.

questions.stem: You say that you plan to rest at home at the weekend.
questions.explanation: 「しゅうまつは、うちで休むつもりです。」 Resting is something you do, so the place takes 「で」. 「休む」 is the dictionary form 「つもり」 needs.

build.translation: I plan to rest at home at the weekend.

questions.stem: You tell your teacher that you plan to do a part-time job in the winter holidays.
questions.explanation: 「冬休みに、アルバイトをするつもりです。」 「アルバイトをする」 is 'do a part-time job'. 「つもりです」 never takes 「します」 or 「ました」; its past is 「つもりでした」.

build.translation: I plan to do a part-time job in the winter holidays.

questions.stem: You say that you don't plan to do a part-time job this year.
questions.explanation: 「今年は、アルバイトをしないつもりです。」 The negative goes on the verb before 「つもり」: 「しないつもり」. 「つもり」 needs a plain form, so 「しません」 cannot come before it.

build.translation: I don't plan to do a part-time job this year.

questions.stem: You tell a friend that you are thinking you would like to study Japanese at university.
questions.explanation: 「大学で日本語をべんきょうしたいと思っています。」 「〜たい」 goes on the ます-stem, and 「と思っています」 makes it a hope you have held for a while. 「と」 quotes the thought, so 「を」 and 「が」 cannot replace it.

build.translation: I'm thinking I'd like to study Japanese at university.

questions.stem: You ask the teacher to say it again, please.
questions.explanation: 「もういちど言ってください。」 「言う」 ends in 「う」, so its て-form is 「言って」. 「もういちど」 is an adverb and needs no particle.

build.translation: Please say it once more.

questions.stem: You ask a Japanese visitor to speak slowly, please.
questions.explanation: 「ゆっくり話してください。」 「話す」 ends in 「す」, so its て-form is 「話して」. 「ゆっくり」 describes how to speak and takes no particle.

build.translation: Please speak slowly.

questions.stem: At the front desk, you ask a visitor to write their name here.
questions.explanation: 「ここに名前を書いてください。」 Writing puts the name on to a place, so 「ここに」. 「書く」 becomes 「書いて」.

build.translation: Please write your name here.

questions.stem: You ask a friend to wait in front of the station.
questions.explanation: 「駅の前でまってください。」 Waiting is an action, so the place takes 「で」. 「まつ」 ends in 「つ」, so its て-form is 「まって」.

build.translation: Please wait in front of the station.

questions.stem: The room is hot, so you ask a friend to open the window.
questions.explanation: 「まどをあけてください。」 「あける」 is the verb for opening something, and it takes 「を」. 「あいて」 comes from 「あく」, which means the window opens by itself.

build.translation: Please open the window.

questions.stem: You ask everyone on the excursion to come a little before eight o'clock.
questions.explanation: 「八時ちょっと前に来てください。」 「八時ちょっと前」 is one time expression, so 「に」 goes once, at its end. 「来る」 is irregular: 「来て」 (きて).

build.translation: Please come a little before eight o'clock.

questions.stem: A friend asks about the school camp. You say that it was very fun.
questions.explanation: 「キャンプはとてもたのしかったです。」 An い-adjective takes its own past: 「たのしかった」. 「たのしいでした」 puts the past on 「です」, which is wrong.

build.translation: The camp was very fun.

questions.stem: You say that the film was not very interesting.
questions.explanation: 「えいがはあまりおもしろくなかったです。」 「あまり」 with a negative is 'not very'. The past negative of an い-adjective is 「〜くなかった」.

options: おもしろくなかったです。
おもしろいじゃなかったです。
おもしろくないでした。

build.translation: The film wasn't very interesting.

questions.stem: You say that the weather was good, so you swam at the beach.
questions.explanation: 「天気がよかったから、うみでおよぎました。」 The past of 「いい」 is 「よかった」, built on 「よ」. Swimming is an action, so 「うみで」.

build.translation: The weather was good, so I swam at the beach.

questions.stem: You ask a friend how the school trip was.
questions.explanation: 「しゅうがくりょこうはどうでしたか。」 「どう」 asks 'how', and 「でしたか」 puts the question in the past because the trip is over.

options: しゅうがくりょこうを
しゅうがくりょこうに
しゅうがくりょこうは

build.translation: How was the school trip?

questions.stem: You tell a friend that at the party you did things like playing games and singing.
questions.explanation: 「パーティーで、ゲームをしたり、うたったりしました。」 Each verb takes 「たり」 on its plain past, and 「しました」 closes the list. 「うたう」 ends in 「う」, so its past is 「うたった」.

build.translation: At the party, we did things like playing games and singing.

questions.stem: You give your opinion that the train is more convenient than the bus.
questions.explanation: 「電車はバスよりべんりだと思います。」 「より」 marks what is being compared against. A な-adjective needs 「だ」 before 「と思います」: 「べんりだと」.

build.translation: I think the train is more convenient than the bus.

questions.stem: You tell a friend that you like tennis more than football.
questions.explanation: 「わたしはサッカーよりテニスのほうが好きです。」 「より」 follows the loser and 「のほうが」 the winner. 「好き」 is a な-adjective, so it ends in 「です」, never 「ます」.

build.translation: I like tennis more than football.

questions.stem: You ask a friend what they think of the new teacher.
questions.explanation: 「新しい先生をどう思いますか。」 「どう思いますか」 asks for an opinion, and the person you have an opinion about takes 「を」.

build.translation: What do you think of the new teacher?

questions.stem: You suggest that going by train would be best.
questions.explanation: 「電車で行くのがいいと思います。」 「の」 turns 「電車で行く」 into a noun, 'going by train', and 「がいいと思います」 recommends it.

build.translation: I think going by train would be good.

questions.stem: A friend gives an opinion and you agree with it.
questions.explanation: 「わたしもそう思います。」 「も」 is 'too', and 「そう」 refers back to what your friend just said.

build.translation: I think so too.
